Pakistani naval ship collides with Indian warship in Arabian SeaIndia summons Pakistan's top diplomat to lodge protest over the incident in the Arabian Sea

The Indian Navy ship was on a routine mission in the North Arabian Sea when the incident occurred | File Photo

Satarupa BhattacharjyaNew Delhi

Listen to This Article

In a rare incident in the Arabian Sea in recent years, a Pakistan Navy ship collided with an Indian Navy warship that was on a regular surveillance mission in the Arabian Sea, not too far from Oman, on Tuesday evening, sources in the Ministry of Defence said on Wednesday.

 

While the sources did not reveal the names of the ships involved in Tuesday’s incident, the Pakistani ship is thought to be the PNS Hunain, a Yarmook-class corvette, which was commissioned in 2024.

 

The Pakistani naval ship “closed in” on the Indian warship, which is larger in size, some 120-130 nautical miles east of the Oman coast, the sources said, adding that it came in “at high speed, manoeuvring in an unprofessional and unsafe manner. This led to a collision” at sea. No structural damage to the Indian warship was reported, the sources said.

 

Earlier on Wednesday, India summoned Saad Ahmad Warraich, the charge d’affaires of the Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi, to lodge a strong protest over the incident.

 

A Ministry of External Affairs media statement said it was the “unacceptable and unprofessional conduct of Pakistani naval units at sea that led to a collision with a unit of the Indian Navy”. While the incident, which took place in international waters, did not cause any major damage, the conduct of the Pakistani naval ship was “in direct contravention” of Article 10 of the Agreement between India and Pakistan on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements of April 1991, the statement said.

Also Read

India has asked Pakistan to respect the relevant agreements between the two sides “to prevent any repeat of such incidents”.

 

This agreement, among other things, stipulates that India and Pakistan would avoid holding major military exercises and manoeuvres in close proximity, be it on land, in water or in the air. It says that both sides would give advance notice to one another on exercises, manoeuvres and troop movements, so as to prevent any situation from arising out of a misreading of each other’s intentions.

 

Usually, naval ships operating in international waters maintain a distance of at least 2-3 nautical miles from each other. In this case, the Pakistani ship approached the Indian warship “aggressively” but “could not break away” at the last moment without making contact,  the sources said. They said the Pakistan Navy did not show respect for the confidence-building measure put in place in 1991, but it also did not demonstrate the capability to manoeuvre when needed.

The Indian Navy has maintained, on average, three or four ships each day in the Arabian Sea over the past months since the war in West Asia between the United States (and Israel) and Iran started, and amid ongoing blockades of the Strait of Hormuz, mostly to escort Indian-flagged commercial vessels transiting through parts of the sea.

 

At the time of the incident, the Indian warship was in the Gulf of Oman (in the northern Arabian Sea), which connects the Indian Ocean to the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz.

 

Unlike in the South China Sea, where incidents involving Chinese ships and those of some other countries with which China has maritime disputes have often been reported over the past decade, the last Pakistan-India naval incident in the Arabian Sea was reported in 2011. Pakistani warship PNS Babur then made contact with INS Godavari, an Indian frigate, while on piracy patrol.
